explanation: The Annual Financial Statement of Art. 112 is popularly called the Budget; the Finance Bill and Treasury Bills are different instruments.

explanation: Art. 266(3) says no moneys out of the CFI shall be appropriated except in accordance with law – Parliament's sanction (with Art. 114(3)); 176, 186 and 386 are irrelevant.

explanation: The State Contingency Fund is at the disposal of, and operated by, the Governor (Art. 267(2)) – not the President, CM or CAG.

q: Who of the following can advance money out of the Contingency Fund of India to meet unforeseen expenses?
options: The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
explanation: The Contingency Fund of India is at the disposal of the President, who makes advances out of it for unforeseen expenditure pending Parliament's authorisation (Art. 267(1)).

notes.text: - **Contingency Fund of India:** created by **Parliament by law** – **Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950**; at the **President's disposal**, who **advances** money for **unforeseen** expenditure (also additional/excess needs) **pending authorisation** by Parliament – spent **before** Parliament's approval. explanation: All revenues received by the Union by taxes and other receipts are credited to the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 266(1)).

explanation: SC judges' salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and HC judges' salaries on the Consolidated Fund of the State – both are Consolidated Funds; there is no 'Special Budget' or 'Amalgamated' fund.

q: The following expenditure shall be charged on the consolidated fund of India, except
options: Debt charges for which the government of India is liable
Salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of Supreme Court judges
The pensions payable to or in respect of judges of any high court
The pensions payable to or in respect of governors of any state
key_text: The pensions payable to or in respect of governors of any state
explanation: Debt charges, SC judges' salaries and HC judges' pensions are charged on the CFI (Art. 112(3)); Governors' emoluments are charged on the State's Consolidated Fund and governors' pensions are not in Art. 112(3).

notes.text: - **Governor:** emoluments charged on the **Consolidated Fund of the State** (Art. 158(3)), not the CFI; one Governor for two or more States → shared in the proportion the **President** fixes by order (**Art. 158(3A)**). Governors' pensions are not in Art. 112(3).

q:
In the context of the enactment of Budget, which of the following statement / statements is / are valid?
I. The Appropriation Bill carries an automatic repeal clause.
II. The provision ' Vote on Account ' has become ineffectual after the re-scheduling of the budget cycle from the last day of February to the first day of February.
III. Amendments to either reject or reduce a tax can not be moved in case of the Finance Bill.
IV. The expenditure charged on the Consolidated 47. Fund of India can only be discussed.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
explanation: I is correct – since the Appropriation Act, 2016 Appropriation Acts carry an automatic repeal (sunset) clause; IV is correct – charged expenditure is only discussed. II is wrong (vote on account is still used in election years) and III is wrong (amendments to reduce or abolish a tax can be moved to the Finance Bill).

notes.text: - **Since the 1 February Budget (2017)** a vote on account is normally needed only in **election years** (with an Interim Budget) – it has not become ineffectual.

- **Charged expenditure** = expenditure from the CFI that the Constitution makes **non-votable** – **not submitted to the vote** of Parliament but **can be discussed** in either House (Art. 113(1)); it still needs an Appropriation Act (Art. 114).

explanation: An advance grant for part of the year pending the regular passage of the Budget is a vote on account (Art. 116); a token grant is for re-appropriation and a vote of credit a blank cheque.

notes.text: - **No parliamentary committee on Welfare of Minorities** (there are committees on Public Undertakings, Government Assurances, Estimates; OBC welfare is an LS committee).

- **Welfare of SCs and STs** is itself a standing committee (30 = 20 LS + 10 RS; **Ministers cannot serve**; examines the reports of the **National Commissions for SCs and STs** and welfare programmes) – it is the **only one of PAC / Estimates / COPU / SC-ST that is not a financial committee**.

q: Who recommended the creation of Committee on Public Undertakings of Indian Parliament?
explanation: The Committee on Public Undertakings was created in 1964 on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee.

notes.text: - **Watchdog group** (NextGen): Subordinate Legislation, Government Assurances, Estimates, PAC, COPU, DRSCs – **not** the Business Advisory Committee.

q: The Anti-Defection Law applies to which of the following in India?
options: Only Members of the Rajya Sabha
explanation: The Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985) covers members of both Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislatures, so both MPs and MLAs.

notes.text: - **Applies to:** members of **both Houses of Parliament and the State Legislatures** (MPs and MLAs, incl. **MLCs**) – party, **independent** and **nominated** members.

q: Which of the following is a feature of Anti-Defection Law?
options: The Tenth Schedule was added to the Constitution by the 44th Amendment Act, which aimed to curb political defections.
Anti-defection law is not applicable in presidential election.
The procedure for disqualifying a member on the grounds of defection is identical to the process used when a person is disqualified for holding an office of profit.
Under the rules established by the Anti-Defection Law, the presiding officer has the authority to initiate a defection case on their own, even without a formal complaint.
key_text: Anti-defection law is not applicable in presidential election.
explanation: The anti-defection law does not apply to the presidential election: the Tenth Schedule covers voting in the House, and parties cannot issue binding whips for the electoral college. It was added by the 52nd (not 44th) Amendment, defection is decided by the presiding officer (office of profit by President on ECI opinion), and he acts only on a petition, not suo motu.

notes.text: - **Not applicable to the presidential election:** the Schedule covers voting **in the House**; no binding whip operates in the electoral college.

q: If a party has 100 legislators (MLAs) in an assembly, as per anti-defection law, how many members are required to create a break-away faction without attracting disqualification?
options: None – no split is protected since 2003 (only a merger by 67 escapes)
key_text: None – no split is protected since 2003 (only a merger by 67 escapes)
explanation:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (None – no split is protected since 2003 (only a merger by 67 escapes)); it is added as option 5.
the one-third split exception (34 of 100) was deleted by the 91st Amendment, 2003 — now no split is protected; only a two-thirds merger (67 of 100) escapes (Rocket Polity #77)
Since the 91st Amendment (2003) deleted the one-third split exception, no break-away faction of any size escapes disqualification; only a merger backed by two-thirds (67 of 100) is protected. 34 (one-third) was the answer under the pre-2003 law, and 30, 33 and 35 were never right.

notes.text: - Number test: party of **100** MLAs – no break-away faction is protected now; a merger needs **67**. **34** (one-third) was the pre-2003 answer.

q: Under the Tenth Schedule of Indian constitution, a legislator will not be disqualified for defection if at least what fraction of the members of a party decide to merge with another party?
explanation: A legislator is not disqualified if two-thirds of the legislature party agree to merge the party with another (Para 4).

q: Which of the following statements is correct about the Anti-Defection Law?
options: The Anti-Defection Law protects members from disqualification in cases where one-third of the members of a legislative party split to form a new group.
A person disqualified on the grounds of defection can become a Minister if he belongs to the ruling party.

If a nominated member fails to join a political party within 6 months of commencement of his term, it is considered as grounds for disqualification of the member of a House of the State Legislature under the Tenth schedule of the constitution.
Disqualification on the grounds of defection does not apply when a member goes out of his party as a result of a merger of the party with another party.
key_text: Disqualification on the grounds of defection does not apply when a member goes out of his party as a result of a merger of the party with another party.
explanation: Disqualification does not apply when a member goes out of his party as a result of a merger (Para 4). The one-third split exception was deleted in 2003; a disqualified defector cannot become a Minister till re-elected (Art. 75(1B)/164(1B)); a nominated member is disqualified only if he joins a party after six months, not for failing to join.

notes.text: - **Merger (Para 4, in force):** no disqualification when the **original party merges** with another and **not less than two-thirds** of its legislature party agree.

- **Statements commonly marked wrong:** "one-third split protects" ✗; "disqualified defector can become a Minister" ✗; "nominated member who fails to join a party in six months is disqualified" ✗; "expelled member loses his seat" ✗; "Speaker not disqualified if he joins another party" ✗.

q: Regarding the provisions related to disqualification on grounds of defection, choose the wrong answer
options: A member of the house belonging to any political party has voluntarily given up his membership of such party would be disqualified
Votes or abstain from voting in such house contrary to any direction issued by the political party to which he belongs would lead to disqualification
A nominated member of a House shall be disqualified for being a member of the house if he joins any political party after the expiration of six months from the date on which he takes his seat
If a party expel a legislator from the party, expelled member loses his seat in the house
key_text: If a party expel a legislator from the party, expelled member loses his seat in the house
explanation: An expelled member does not lose his seat: he continues to belong to the party for Tenth Schedule purposes (G. Viswanathan 1996) and sits as unattached. Giving up membership, defying the whip and a nominated member joining a party after six months are grounds of disqualification.

notes.text: - **Expelled member:** does **not lose his seat**; he still belongs to the party for Tenth Schedule purposes (G. Viswanathan 1996) and sits as unattached; joining another party then = giving up membership.

q: Regarding anti defection, which of the following is not correct?
options: If a member defects from one party to some other party he is disqualified by the speaker
If a party expels an elected member of the party, the Member does not lose his seat in Legislature immediately
If a group of one-Third of members of the party decided to split, they will not lose their seats

key_text: If a group of one-Third of members of the party decided to split, they will not lose their seats
explanation: Since the 91st Amendment (2003) a one-third split no longer protects members, so that statement is not correct. A defector is disqualified by the Speaker, an expelled member keeps his seat, and a two-thirds merger is protected.

notes.text: - **Split (Para 3, one-third):** **deleted by the 91st Amendment (2003)** – a one-third group that breaks away is now disqualified.

q: Regarding the privileges of the parliament, choose the wrong answer?
options: Constitution guaranteed freedom of speech in parliament
The Members of parliament are immune from arrest in Civil cases whether the parliament is in session or not.
In Criminal cases parliament members cannot be arrested while they are in the House in Session
Parliament has freedom to publish its proceedings
key_text: The Members of parliament are immune from arrest in Civil cases whether the parliament is in session or not.
explanation: Freedom from arrest applies only in civil cases and only during a session and 40 days before and after it, not 'whether Parliament is in session or not'. Free speech (Art. 105(1)), the right to publish proceedings and the rule that no member is arrested within the precincts without the presiding officer's permission are all correct.
